6.text:
Async Swap is an MEV-capturing DEX: an on-chain order book and matching engine built as a Uniswap
v4 hook. Value that searchers usually take from ordering and backruns goes to the protocol and LPs
instead. Traders set a
limit price for assets paired with USDC. Orders match with other traders or with the pool's active
liquidity, and anyone can permissionlessly fill a resting order. Price, then bid, then time. Book matching ranks orders by price. Among orders at the same
price, a higher escrowed USDC priority bid goes first, and earlier orders break equal bids.Ordering MEV is auctioned, not extracted. Priority bids are paid in USDC to the protocol's
FeeVault, so jumping the queue at a price costs the bidder, not other traders.Backruns pay LPs. Each pool's first fill in a 2-block window records the price before it. A
later fill in that window that moves the same pool's price back toward it pays a dynamic fee of
about half the backrun's profit, split between LPs and the protocol. Other pools are unaffected.
See dynamic fee ordering.Orders rest until they execute. Unfilled amounts stay open for later matching, a pool fill,
a filler, repricing or cancellation.No swap touches the curve directly. Every swap becomes an order. The only AMM swaps are the
ones the hook makes to fill a resting order from pool liquidity, and those pay active LPs
0.02% and the protocol 0.01%. Book matches and filler fills take 0.02% of what each side receives.Proceeds you can always claim. A book match credits both sides as PoolManager claims, which
you redeem to any address through TokenClaims (ERC-20) or NativeClaims (ETH), or to your own
wallet through Router.withdrawClaims. A recipient a token refuses cannot block matching.Rules the owner cannot change. Anyone can open a USDC pool on the hook. The minimum order, the
$0.10 priority-bid cap and the 0.0001-token asset floor are fixed when the hook is deployed; the
owner can only collect fees, sweep stranded balances and transfer ownership.Batch your actions. Router.multicall cancels several orders and withdraws claims in one
atomic transaction, with no extra approvals.

Git Source Inherits: EIP712, Multicall Title: Router Author: @msakiart Thin entrypoint for makers (swap, topUpPriorityFee, cancelOrder, cancelAndWithdraw, withdrawClaims), fillers
(fillOrder) and keepers (matchBook, fillFromPoolLiquidity), batched with multicall. Each action
goes through IPoolManager.unlock so the hook can operate on PM debts. Native payouts/refunds are
PoolManager claims (ID 0), redeemable through NativeClaims or withdrawClaims; ERC20 payouts remain
direct. Gasless variants (swapWithSig, cancelWithSig) take the maker's EIP-712 signature so a
relayer can submit. Signed creates pull input through Permit2 with the order as witness,
so the wallet shows the full order (tokens, amounts, pool) in one readable message. multicall runs several of these as one atomic transaction, each as the caller (for example,
cancel many orders and withdraw the claims). It is not payable, so native-value actions
(swap with native input, fillOrder with native output) cannot reuse one msg.value.
Each action keeps its own PoolManager unlock and sets the transient slots it reads. Order creation and fills (swap, swapWithSig, fillOrder, fillFromPoolLiquidity) pay an MEV tax
("Priority Is All You Need", Robinson & White): mevTax(), the transaction's priority fee per gas times
MEV_TAX_GAS, in ETH on top of any native deposit, credited to the FeeVault as native claims. On a chain
that orders by priority fee, searchers racing for the same position bid it up, so most of what they race
for goes to the protocol; a transaction with no priority pays nothing. Inside multicall, which is not
payable, a taxed action needs a transaction with no priority.
Flash fills (fillOrderWithCallback) charge the tax per fill as a PoolManager debt instead; see
IAsyncSwapCallback.

512.text: The protocol overview has the short order sequence; this page has the detailed ones. See order lifecycle and priority bids for the flowcharts, flash fills for the flash-fill sequence and Dutch auctions for auction fills. Solid arrows are calls or actions; dashed arrows are returns or delivered results. Each sequence groups related transactions; it is not one transaction from top to bottom. The app and wallet represent the user interface, not trusted settlement components. An indexer may observe emitted events for discovery, but neither an API nor an indexer is required by the contracts. IncomingMatching, AsyncMatching, MultiAsset and DutchAuction are linked libraries called by DELEGATECALL in the hook's context, and AsyncFiller is internal to them, so arrows from them to PoolManager execute as the hook. ERC-6909 claims and LP fee accounting live inside PoolManager. Every Router action is one PoolManager.unlock (v4 flash accounting): it can only finish once every delta is zero.

Later fill in the window that moves the price back toward it: half the price gap it closes. opt Dynamic fee is due Fee->>PM: donate half of the fee to in-range LPs Fee->>PM: mint the rest to FeeVault as claims end Fee-->>Match: Dynamic fee, taken from the output alt Full remaining input consumed and minimum output met after the dynamic fee Match->>PM: Pay output less the dynamic fee, settle remaining bid to FeeVault PM-->>Wallet: ERC-20 proceeds or native claims Match-->>Hook: Order removed, liquidity fill event else Pool first, stopped at the book level, pro-rata minimum met Match->>Match: Reduce the order, keeping the maker's limit, and settle the filled bid share Match->>PM: Credit output less the dynamic fee as claims Match-->>Hook: Order stays open for the book, liquidity fill event else Insufficient liquidity, partial execution without a limit, or limit not met Match-->>Hook: Self-call reverts, caught by matchNewOrder Note over Hook,PM: Only LP attempt rolls back, prior book fills and open remainder survive. end end Hook-->>Router: Matched pair count Router-->>PM: Callback complete PM-->>Router: Unlock completes if all currency deltas are settled Router-->>Wallet: Direct transaction succeeds Note over Wallet,Relayer: For signed submission, the transaction result returns to the submitter instead. 514.text:
These are alternative actions on open orders. Private fills and LP retries require the Router to remain authorized by the maker. 516.text:
A maker can open a resting order with a short Dutch auction. The order rests in the book at the maker's minimum
output, the floor, the whole time. On top of it, flash fillers pay a premium that starts high and falls in a
straight line to zero. Fillers fill as soon as the total works for them, so the maker gets the best price they
compete for. When the auction ends the premium is zero and the order is a plain good-till-cancelled order at the
floor. Nothing has to be stepped, and no keeper is needed. The logic lives in the linked DutchAuction library; the
auction record is stored in the hook by order id.

520.text:
A large order that fills against pool liquidity moves the pool price. Whoever trades the price back
earns the difference: a backrun. With only a static fee, that profit goes entirely to the
backrunner, and the LPs whose liquidity absorbed both trades lose it. Since v1.1.0, dynamic fee
ordering charges a pool fill that moves the price back a dynamic fee sized to the gap it closes,
and splits it between the LPs and the protocol. The dynamic fee applies only to pool fills (fillFromPoolLiquidity, including the pool attempt when a
new order arrives). Book matches and filler fills settle at the orders' signed limits, move no pool
price and don't pay it.
520.title: Dynamic fee ordering

521.text:
The logic is in DynamicFeeOrdering.sol, a linked library
that AsyncMatching calls after every pool fill. Reference. Each pool stores a reference tick and the block it was set in
(AsyncFiller.State.refTick, refBlock). The first pool fill after the window has expired records
the pool's tick from before that fill as the new reference, and pays no dynamic fee.Window. The reference holds for ORDERING_WINDOW = 2 blocks after the block that set it. A
pool fill after that starts a new window.Dynamic fee. A pool fill inside the window that ends closer to the reference than it started
paysfee = min(amountOut × (gapBefore + gapAfter) / 40_000, amountOut / 2)where gapBefore and gapAfter are the distances, in ticks, from the reference to the pool's tick
before and after the fill. If the fill crosses the reference, gapAfter is 0 and amountOut is only
the share of the output from the side before the reference, amountOut × gapBefore / (gapBefore +
ticks past the reference): the part past the reference closes no gap and pays nothing. One tick is about 0.01%, so (gapBefore + gapAfter) / 2 is the average
price gap over the fill in basis points, and the fee is half the price gap the fill closes.No dynamic fee for a fill that moves the price further from the reference, or doesn't move it.Split. Half the dynamic fee is donated to in-range LPs (PoolManager.donate). The other half,
plus any rounding, is credited to the FeeVault as ERC-6909 claims. If no liquidity is in range
after the fill, all of it goes to the FeeVault.Maker protection. The dynamic fee is taken from the fill's output before the maker is paid, and
the output that remains must still meet the order's minimum. Otherwise the pool fill reverts, and
the order goes to the book or rests, exactly as when a pool fill misses its limit for any other
reason. The 0.01% protocol fee on the input and the 0.02% LP fee still apply to every pool fill; the dynamic
fee is on top of them. Each charge emits DynamicFeeCharged(poolId, orderId, currency, toLps, toFeeVault, refTick) from the
hook: the fill's output currency, the LPs' and the FeeVault's shares, and the reference tick it was
measured against. The fill's AsyncOrderLiquidityFilled reports the maker's output after the fee. Every successful pool fill also emits PoolPriceObserved(poolId, orderId, tickBefore, tickAfter, refTick, observedBlock). Indexers can use these events as a price-movement log to identify large tick moves and evaluate fee settings. The contract stores only the current reference tick and block; it does not need a full on-chain price history to calculate the fee, which continues to scale with the tick gap the fill closes.

522.title: Example

523.text:
A fee charged per swap invites splitting: several small backruns each pay a lower rate. Here the
dynamic fee depends on the gap at each fill's start and end, not on how many fills there are.
Splitting one backrun into several orders pays roughly the same total, because each piece pays on the
part of the gap it closes. In the test, five orders earn 1.38 USDC against 1.34 for one; the small
difference comes from averaging the gap linearly in ticks while the pool's price curve is not linear.

524.text:
The dynamic fee is in the output currency. A backrun that buys the asset pays it in the asset;
one that sells the asset pays in USDC. Valued at the reference price, the two are the same.Only within the window. A backrun that lands more than 2 blocks after the fill that set the
reference pays nothing. On chains with short block times, such as Unichain, that's a few seconds.One reference per window. If several large fills happen in one window, they're all measured
against the price before the first one.It's an estimate. The gap is measured in ticks against the pool's own earlier price, not against
an outside market price. A fill that moves the pool back after the outside market really moved
still pays within the window.Not in formal proofs. The Foundry tests and the uv4 Python model cover it.

526.text:
A flash fill lets a filler fill an order with no inventory. The Router gives the filler the order's escrowed input
first, as ERC-6909 claims, calls the filler back inside its own PoolManager.unlock, and only then collects the
maker's output. Inside the callback the filler can swap on any Uniswap v4 pool, fill other Async Swap orders with
fillOrderInCallback, and run matchBookInCallback, in a loop it controls. This is v4 flash accounting: nothing
has to be funded up front, as long as every delta is zero when the unlock ends.

545.text:
Every resting order is indexed on its pool's book by a uint128 price key computed in
AsyncFiller._priceKey (TickPrice.key): the Uniswap v4 tick of the order's exact limit. Take the order's currency1/currency0 ratio: amountOutMin / amountIn when it sells currency0,
amountIn / amountOutMin when it sells currency1.Take its floor tick: the largest tick t (spacing 1, price 1.0001^t) priced at or below the
ratio (TickPrice.floorTick, via TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice).Order ticks by numeraire per asset: t - MIN_TICK + 1 when the numeraire is currency1,
MAX_TICK - t + 1 when it is currency0. Keys run from 1 to 2 * MAX_TICK + 1. Ratios outside the v4 price range (about 2^-128 to
2^128) share the end keys. Each level is 0.01% wide at any price and for any token decimals,
so two orders sharing a nonclamped key are within approximately 0.01% of each other.
The end levels do not have this spread bound. The exact limit stays on the order:
keys order the radix tree; they do not by themselves decide whether two orders trade.

546.title: Price keys

547.text:
AsyncMatching._crosses(buyKey, sellKey, buy, sell) decides whether a buy and a sell can trade: buyKey > sellKey is a cross and buyKey < sellKey is not. The key is monotone in the exact
price, so a strict ordering of keys always reflects a strict ordering of exact prices.Equal keys are decided at full precision: cross  <=>  buyIn / buyOut >= sellOut / sellIn
       <=>  buyIn * sellIn >= sellOut * buyOut
       <=>  floor(buyIn * sellIn / sellOut) >= buyOut      (sellOut and buyOut are nonzero) implemented as Math.mulDiv(buy.amountIn, sell.amountIn, sell.amountOutMin) >= buy.amountOutMin.
Orders cannot be created or updated with a zero minimum, so the divisor is never zero. Both escrowed inputs are bounded by signed 128-bit settlement amounts, so their product and
its quotient by a positive minimum fit in 256 bits, including at clamped end levels. An exact tie (buyIn * sellIn == sellOut * buyOut) counts as a cross and executes.
547.title: Crossing rule

548.text:
Equal-key noncrossing heads no longer terminate selection when another pair is eligible.
Each priority subtree stores its minimum exact ask or maximum exact bid. The search chooses
the higher-priority child if its summary admits a crossing order, otherwise the other child.
Each lookup traverses at most 128 branches without scanning or persistent cursors.Automatic arrivals and resting-book matching use the same selection rule: the exact highest
bid and exact lowest ask in their best levels. The subtree extremum is the eligibility threshold,
so only orders at that exact extremum qualify; remaining fee and sequence break exact-price ties.
If these extrema do not cross, no pair at the boundary crosses. Prices grouped in the same level
never let a worse exact price jump ahead by paying more.Every genuine cross, including the tie, produces a non-zero match in _matchAmounts that pays
each maker at least their signed minimum for the input consumed. This was checked exhaustively
for small amounts and on randomized large near-tie pairs.Matching compares the signed minimums, not the post-fee proceeds, so the 0.02% trade fee (taken
from each side's proceeds afterwards, rounded up) never changes which orders cross. Example of equal keys without a cross: a sell asking 1000.05 and a buy offering 1000.02
USDC per asset sit on the same tick, but the buy is below the ask, so the pair rests.
548.title: Consequences

550.text:
Within one tick, priority is bid then sequence, not exact price, so a higher-bid order can trade
ahead of one priced up to 0.01% better. Across ticks, price always comes first. Under the earlier
WAD-ratio key a level was 10^(assetDecimals - usdcDecimals - 18) USDC/asset wide, which is
about 10% of the price for an 18-decimal asset at $0.00001, and the clamped keys 1 and
type(uint128).max merged arbitrarily distant prices (audit 2026-10-23, finding 1). Ticks remove
both: the width is relative and fixed, and only prices outside the v4 range share the end keys.
550.title: Level width and the price-priority bound

551.text:
test/security/CoarsePriceBlocking.t.sol creates a pool with an 18-decimal asset and 6-decimal
USDC fixture at 1,000 USDC/asset, minimum order 1 USDC, and no active LP liquidity. A sell
offering 2e15 - 1 asset base units for 2_000_000 USDC base units has the same key as a
1,000 USDC/asset order, but a slightly higher exact ask. Its 100_001-unit bid outranks the
100_000-unit bids of 20 honest sells. Under the previous head-only policy, twenty matching buys stopped at that blocker, and 100
retries made no progress. The Python legacy_matching=True mode preserves that baseline. With exact eligibility, the same twenty buys execute against the honest sells without cancelling
or outbidding the blocker. The blocker remains open, preserving its escrow and bid. The updated
CoarsePriceBlockingTest asserts that outcome through the real Router/hook/PoolManager, and tests
the mirrored incoming-sell case. Generated EligiblePythonVectors.t.sol exercises normal prices,
both clamps, blockers on both sides, mutations, partial fills, balances and fee claims. With tick keys the blocker above is one level worse than the honest asks, so it cannot outrank
them at all. A level is 0.01% of the price wide. That bounds price separation, not delay or backlog.
The repaired selector guarantees finding a crossing pair in a valid book when one exists;
successful settlement and transaction submission remain required. It does not guarantee that
every low-priority order eventually fills under continuing higher-priority arrivals. The companion model is in the local uv4 checkout under src/uv4/priority_protocol/, with results
and explicit modeling boundaries in docs/priority_protocol/. PriorityPythonVectors.t.sol checks
100 independently generated Python matching cases against the real matcher;
PriorityPythonHashes.t.sol checks order identities and signature struct hashes.

552.text:
EligiblePrice.sol compares full 512-bit cross products and stores two-word exact bounds at
priority-tree nodes. Append/remove repair the affected ancestor path. Every partial fill refreshes
the bound even if neither the tick key nor the remaining fee changes. New storage is appended
to each price level; existing live trees would need their summaries initialized before using this
code. These local changes have not been deployed. The protocol-controlled index work is O(128 M) for M matches. Eight is the existing per-call cap,
not a per-transaction cap. Token code and external settlement costs are outside this structural
bound. EligibleGas.t.sol measures composed batches through a real unlock; no numerical
worst-case gas certificate or universally optimal batch size is claimed. The updated whitepaper is in the local asyncswap/whitepaper checkout. Its new section contains
integer safety and search arguments, gas curves, and the constrained parameter objective.

553.title: Priority fee top-ups

554.text:
router.topUpPriorityFee(order, addedFee); The caller must be order.owner, with sufficient USDC balance and ERC-20 allowance to the Router.
A registered filling executor cannot top up another maker's order. Agents can submit from the maker's
wallet or through that wallet's own authorized execution mechanism. There is no new relayed signature
or Permit2 top-up endpoint in this version. addedFee is a positive delta in the numeraire's base units. With six-decimal USDC, 25_000 adds
$0.025. The function identifies the order by chain, pool, owner, direction and salt; the amount,
minimum output and fee supplied in the order struct may be stale. It adds to the bid currently stored
on the order. For example, a $0.10 bid reduced to $0.075 by a partial fill becomes $0.10 after adding
$0.025. The resulting bid must be at least min(remaining USDC notional / 1000, pool priorityFeeCap), rounded
down. The default cap is $0.10 and limits the required minimum, not the user's maximum bid. A partially
consumed bid may sit below this minimum until amended, but a top-up must bring it back to the current
minimum. The resulting bid cannot exceed uint64.max base units. Missing and closed orders revert.
554.title: API

555.text:
The limit price and remaining input budget do not change.Exact price remains the first ranking rule. A higher bid breaks equal-price ties.The order receives a fresh queue sequence and joins behind existing equal-price, equal-fee orders.The original maker age and signed reprice version stay unchanged. A pending signed reprice or
cancellation is not invalidated by a top-up; nonce invalidation remains the way to revoke it.Added fees follow the existing non-refundable settlement rule: proportional consumption on fills,
with the remainder going to the FeeVault on closure or cancellation. They are not keeper rewards. The Router transfers USDC to PoolManager and credits the hook before the library rekeys the fee
queue and mints the added escrow claims. The price-level bitmap and order counts stay unchanged.
PoolManager requires balanced currency deltas at unlock completion; a payment failure, short payment
or invalid amendment reverts funding and queue changes together. The hook emits: event AsyncOrderPriorityFeeUpdated(
    PoolId indexed poolId, bytes32 indexed orderId, uint256 addedFee, uint256 newPriorityFee
); The update uses the live order after payment. If a token callback partially fills it, the delta is
added to that remainder; if the order closes during payment, the transaction reverts. Supported USDC
transfers do not normally make such callbacks, but this behavior is tested.
555.title: Priority and settlement

556.text:
A top-up does not attempt matching and does not pay the Router's native MEV tax. It still costs
transaction gas. Use it when raising priority for future liquidity. When compatible liquidity is
already visible, combine it with a bounded matching call: bytes[] memory calls = new bytes[](https://github.com/asyncswap/contracts/blob/main/docs/2);
calls[0] = abi.encodeCall(router.topUpPriorityFee, (order, addedFee));
calls[1] = abi.encodeCall(router.matchBook, (order.key, uint8(8)));
router.multicall(calls); maxMatches must be 1–8. The matcher processes the book's best executable pairs, so the targeted
order is not guaranteed a fill within that bound. If no crossing pair exists, matching may succeed
without a fill and the top-up remains committed. If either call reverts, the entire batch reverts.
This is book matching; LP retries remain the separate fillFromPoolLiquidity path. Read the live remaining bid and order state, choose a spending limit, then simulate the exact call
or multicall before submission. Simulation does not reserve liquidity. Retrying the same successful
top-up in a new transaction adds the delta again; check the receipt and current bid before retrying. For transaction-cost measurements and reproduction instructions, see the top-up benchmark. Sources: Router, hook,
fee amendments, and
tests.

560.text:
Async Swap is a Uniswap v4 hook that turns swaps into limit orders. Makers escrow their input in the hook and set a
minimum output. Every pool pairs an asset with USDC (the numeraire). Orders are filled by matching against each
other, by permissionless fillers, or against the pool's own liquidity. Pools. Anyone can create a pool: the hook accepts one that pairs the configured USDC with an asset that has
code and uses the dynamic-fee flag. The owner cannot open, close or configure pools.Book. Orders sit at price levels on v4 ticks (TickPrice: the floor tick of the exact limit, 0.01% apart).
The outer index is a bounded bitmap. Within a level they rank by exact limit, then escrowed priority bid, then arrival (EligiblePrice); exact
rational limits decide crossing. New orders and any crossed backlog share one book-wide selection, at most eight
pairs per call.Venue choice. A new order goes to the better venue first (TickPrice.poolBeatsLevel). If the pool's price
beats the best opposite level (inside the dynamic-fee window, counting the fee a fill back toward the reference
would pay), the pool goes first, limited one tick short of that level and inside v4's price range, and the book
matches the rest. Otherwise the book goes first and the pool must take all of any remainder. A pool fill that
would leave no active liquidity reverts.Fees. Book matches and filler fills take 0.02% from what each side receives. Pool fills pay active LPs 0.02%
and the protocol 0.01%, plus a dynamic fee (DynamicFeeOrdering) on a fill that moves the price back toward the
first pool fill's starting tick within 2 blocks: half the gap it closes, half to LPs and half to FeeVault.Settlement. Book matches credit both sides, and any remainder left below the pool minimum, as PoolManager
ERC-6909 claims, batched per call (ClaimTransfers). Holders redeem them through TokenClaims (ERC-20),
NativeClaims (ETH) or Router.withdrawClaims. Filler fills and full pool fills pay ERC-20 output directly; native
output, and a pool fill that leaves part of the order on the book, are credited as claims.Priority bids. Optional, paid in USDC and escrowed when the order is created. Each fill settles its
proportional share and the rest settles when the order closes. Every settled bid goes to FeeVault, never to LPs. Makers may add funded USDC to the remaining bid through the Router; this changes fee priority without changing their limit price.Minimums. Fixed at deployment, no setter: an optional minimum order in USDC (minOrder, from a dollar amount
and the numeraire's decimals; 0 by default) and an asset floor per pool (minAssetAmount, 10^(decimals − 4), so
0.0001 of a token). The $0.10 bid cap is derived from the numeraire's decimals too.Signed actions. Permit2 order witnesses (swapWithSig), SetExecutor, UpdatePrice (binds the order's
createdSequence and its reprices count; a reprice that lands after partial matches applies its signed price
to the remainder) and CancelOrder (no order size: covers whatever remains). All use unordered nonces in one space.Router. The single trusted entry for order creation, and an executor makers can't revoke. multicall batches
actions as the caller (not payable). Order creation and fills pay an MEV tax of the transaction's priority fee
times MEV_TAX_GAS (per chain, fixed at deployment: 20,000,000 on Unichain and Unichain Sepolia, which order by
priority fee), in msg.value on top of any native deposit, credited to FeeVault as native claims. The Router can
cancel for a maker without an executor grant.

Owner (two-step transferOwnership / acceptOwnership): sweeps tokens sent to the hook by mistake (sweep;
escrow lives in PoolManager claims, not the hook's balance) and collects fees, bids and MEV tax from FeeVault.
It cannot open, close or configure pools or change minimums. Must not be able to take makers' escrow.Router: the hook trusts its immutable router as the only order-creation path, as an executor no maker can
revoke, for grant-free cancels on a maker's behalf (the Router checks the owner or a signature), and for burning
cancel nonces, and for maker-authorized, funded priority-fee amendments. A generic executor grant does not authorize spending a maker's USDC for top-ups.Executors: a maker authorizes executors per pool (setExecutor or setExecutorWithSig) and can revoke any of
them except the Router. An executor can only act on that maker's orders.Fillers / matchers / keepers: anyone; permissionless.Pool creators: anyone, for any asset with code. A malicious asset must only be able to affect its own pool.Tokens: USDC plus standard ERC-20s and native ETH. Fee-on-transfer and rebasing tokens are not supported.

564.text:
Acknowledged in the reviews below: Ways to race without the MEV tax (Pashov 4, 5, 6, 9): a searcher can reprice its own resting order with
updatePrice and settle it with matchBook (on the Router or directly on the hook, which needs no unlock), or
pool-fill its own order through tryFillOrderFromPoolLiquidity with its own contract as executor. No user loses
funds; the tax covers Router creation and fills only.A partly matched order can fall behind an equal-priced order (Pashov 7): the remainder's minimum rounds up, so
its exact limit is one unit worse than the maker signed and its bid buys no priority. Pinned by
test_knownIssue_partlyMatchedOrderFallsBehindAnEqualOrder.Fees round to zero on dust orders (LSP I-01): only with minimums off.The MEV tax needs an exact msg.value: the deposit plus priority fee × MEV_TAX_GAS. Wallets should send taxed
calls with no priority fee; the app does. By design: A top-up is an additive action. Repeating it in a new transaction spends the delta again. It resets fee-tier
age, not maker age, and does not invalidate a previously signed cancellation or reprice. A multicall can
commit a top-up even when matching succeeds with zero fills. These are explicit semantics, not fill guarantees.Makers can't revoke the Router. A maker who wants out cancels its orders (through the Router, by signature,
or directly from its own unlock); the Router acts for a maker only when that maker calls it or signs.Priority bids and top-ups are non-refundable. All of a bid goes to FeeVault, including on cancellation or a dust close.Tokens with recipient callbacks (e.g. ERC-777) are not supported. Matching pays only claims and runs no
recipient code; filler fills and full pool fills transfer ERC-20 output after the order is closed.Proceeds are claims. Recipients redeem through TokenClaims, NativeClaims or Router.withdrawClaims.DeployWithdrawalRouter deploys a testnet-only second Router for claims; the hook trusts only its own Router,
so cancels through the second one fail.MatchingEngine.sol is a benchmark harness, not deployed (AuditAgent finding 8, acknowledged).Release items in MAINNET_READINESS.md (deployment rehearsal, bytecode pinning, throughput stress, deploying the
claim redeemers) are operational, not code findings. The 29 leads in the Pashov review and the leads in the LSP review are unconfirmed trails, not known issues:
confirming or ruling out any of them is in scope.
